id: Gwendolyn Brooks: America in the Wintertime

prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Black, Africa

outputs.L1:
In this moment of orangutans, wolves, and scavengers—of high heat redesigning the North and South Poles; of new tribes wandering in limousines; of the confirmations of liars, thieves, and get-over artists; of the wilderness of Pennsylvania Avenue and Standing Rock; of misspelled executive orders on yellow paper bearing crooked signatures—where are the kind language-makers among us?

At a time of extreme climate damage, of deciphering fake news, alternative truths, and me-ism, you saw the twenty-first century and left us neither of your own accord nor by your own permission. You fought and fought through most of the twentieth century, creating an army of poets who learned and loved language and the stories of complicated rivers, seas, and oceans.

Where is the kind, green nourishment of kale and wheatgrass?

You thought, wrote, and lived poetry. You knew that terror is also language, rooted in denial, first-ism, and rich cowards. You were honey and yes to us. You never ran from Black—as in bones, Africa, blood, and the questioning of yesterdays and tomorrows.

We never saw you dance, but you had rhythm. You were a warrior before the war, creating earth-language, uncommon signs, and melodies, and you did not sing the songs of career slaves. Keenly aware of Tubman, Douglass, Wells-Barnett, Du Bois, and the oversized consciousness and commitment of never-quit people religiously taking note of the bloodlust enemies of kindness, we hear your last words:

“America, if you see me as your enemy, you have no friends.”
outputs.L2:
We inhabit an age of orangutans, wolves, and carrion eaters; an age when fierce heat reshapes both poles and newly formed tribes roam in limousines. Deceivers, criminals, and hustlers receive confirmation amid the wild terrain of Pennsylvania Avenue and Standing Rock, while executive decrees—misspelled, printed on yellow sheets, and marked by twisted signatures—circulate. Where, among us, are the gentle shapers of language?

You glimpsed the twenty-first century during a period of catastrophic climate harm, manufactured news, substitute realities, and rampant self-absorption, then departed without choosing or consenting to leave. Through much of the twentieth century, you struggled relentlessly, assembling generations of poets who came to understand and cherish words, as well as tales of intricate rivers, seas, and oceans. Where can we now find the tender, green sustenance of wheatgrass and kale?

Poetry was how you imagined, wrote, and existed. You understood that terror, too, is constructed through words rooted in refusal, “first” ideologies, and wealthy acts of cowardice. To us, you were sweetness and affirmation. You never turned away from Blackness—in bone, Africa, blood, or the interrogation of what came before and what lies ahead.

We did not witness you dancing, yet rhythm lived within you. Before war arrived, you were already a fighter, inventing a vocabulary of the earth, unexpected symbols, and new music. You refused to perform the anthems of those enslaved by ambition.

You remained sharply conscious of Tubman, Douglass, Wells-Barnett, and Du Bois, and of the immense awareness and devotion of people who would not surrender—people who faithfully recorded the bloodthirsty adversaries of compassion. Now we hear your final declaration: America, if you regard me as an enemy, then you are without friends.
outputs.L3:
The speaker presents the twenty-first century as a period marked by profound moral and social crisis. Climate destruction threatens the planet, while political corruption, misinformation, greed, and selfishness weaken public life and human solidarity. Against this bleak contemporary landscape, the poem mourns a poet who spent much of the twentieth century caring for language, preserving stories, and inspiring successive generations of writers.

The poet’s legacy is defined not only by literary achievement but also by moral courage. In both life and writing, the poet confronted terror, denial, racism, greed, and cowardice, refusing to remain silent in the face of injustice. Deeply rooted in Black history and identity, the poet drew strength from the struggles and examples of figures such as Harriet Tubman, Frederick Douglass, Ida B. Wells-Barnett, and W. E. B. Du Bois. These historical voices helped shape a poetry committed to truth, resistance, dignity, and collective memory.

The poem therefore functions as both an elegy and a warning. It honors a writer whose words offered courage and guidance while also challenging the society that still needs those words. In its closing declaration, the speaker warns that if America continues to treat voices of truth, compassion, and kindness as enemies, it will ultimately isolate itself. A nation that rejects its most honest and humane voices will eventually discover that it has no friends left.
outputs.L4:
The elegy mourns the death of a Black poet-warrior while placing his life and work within the larger crises facing the United States and the world. Its grief is inseparable from political anger: the poem confronts corruption, systemic racism, environmental destruction, and the manipulation of language by those in power. Through urgent images, historical allusions, and direct address, the speaker connects the poet’s death to a long history of oppression and resistance. The poem suggests that distorted language is itself a form of violence, because euphemisms, propaganda, and official lies conceal injustice and weaken society’s ability to recognize the truth.

Against these destructive forces, the elegy presents the poet as a lifelong defender of honesty, compassion, and freedom. His poetry is not treated as a private or merely artistic achievement, but as an active form of struggle—a means of exposing injustice, preserving memory, and imagining liberation. Although his death creates a profound absence, his words and moral example continue to challenge the living. The elegy therefore becomes both a tribute and a warning. By honoring his courage, kindness, and commitment to truth, it insists that his legacy will endure beyond his lifetime. At the same time, it argues that an America that rejects, silences, or persecutes voices like his does not simply isolate its poets; it isolates itself from justice, community, and the possibility of meaningful change.
outputs.L5:
## Black Identity and Africa

Africa is a vast and diverse continent with thousands of cultures, languages, and traditions. It is also the ancestral homeland of many Black communities around the world. From the ancient civilizations of Egypt, Nubia, Mali, and Great Zimbabwe to today’s dynamic cities and creative industries, Africa has profoundly influenced global history and culture.

Black identity cannot be reduced to a single experience. People of African descent live across the continent and throughout the diaspora, including in the Americas, the Caribbean, Europe, and Asia. Their identities are shaped by nationality, ethnicity, language, family, and history.

Despite the lasting effects of slavery, colonialism, and racial discrimination, Black communities have demonstrated extraordinary resilience and creativity. African and diasporic contributions can be seen in literature, science, politics, art, fashion, and music. Recognizing this diversity allows us to celebrate Africa not merely as a place of origin, but as a continent continually shaping the modern world.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a free-verse elegy for a recently deceased Black revolutionary poet, connecting his literary legacy to Trump-era politics, climate change, Standing Rock, fake news, and African American resistance.
counterfactuals.output:
**Elegy with a Match Still Burning**

Brother,  
the microphone keeps your fingerprints.

Even now, after the last breath  
closed its red door,  
your vowels patrol the avenue—  
sirens turned backward,  
drums refusing the museum.

You taught the page  
it was not paper  
but a window broken during curfew,  
a warrant read aloud,  
a fist learning the grammar of sky.

Then came the towered man  
selling fear in a red cap,  
building walls from television,  
calling cruelty order,  
calling cages law,  
calling every wound he opened  
someone else’s fault.

The country clicked *share.*

Truth became a body  
left in the street  
while cameras argued  
whether it had ever been alive.

Fake news, they said,  
as if the lie were newly born—  
as if Black mouths had not long testified  
against official weather:  
the strange rain of bullets,  
the forecast of prisons,  
the white voice calmly announcing  
nothing happened here.

At Standing Rock,  
water protectors faced the winter,  
dogs, floodlights, armored men.  
The river carried an old intelligence:  
no pipeline is only a pipeline,  
no burial ground is empty,  
no empire drills without first  
renaming the sacred.

You would have heard the rhythm—  
boots against prayer,  
hoses against song—  
and found in that frozen air  
the same breath that crossed  
slave-ship dark,  
cotton field, chain gang,  
Harlem fire escape,  
Birmingham cell.

Now glaciers loosen  
their ancient grip.  
Oceans climb the stairs.  
Forests enter the atmosphere as smoke.  
The poorest neighborhoods  
learn the names of storms  
before the rich learn mercy.

Still, your poems do not ask permission.

They rise in classrooms,  
barbershops, buses,  
in the throat of a child  
who has just discovered  
that history is not finished  
and neither is she.

They march beside Douglass and Tubman,  
Du Bois and Wells,  
Baldwin’s blade of witness,  
Nina’s thunder,  
the Panthers’ breakfast tables,  
the mothers who lift photographs  
when the nation lowers its eyes.

We bury you  
but not the match.

We bury the hand  
but not the handwriting.

Somewhere tonight  
a young Black poet bends over a screen  
lit like a small rebellion,  
typing through the algorithm’s fog,  
through slogans, smoke, and surveillance,  
toward a language no wall can hold.

Brother,  
the microphone keeps your fingerprints.

The earth is warming.  
The water remembers.  
The lie has many channels.

But resistance—  
resistance still has your voice.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a prose poem honoring Amiri Baraka as a fearless language maker, cultural warrior, and mentor to generations of poets. Use lowercase lettering, dense historical references, surreal imagery, and political anger.
counterfactuals.output:
amiri, you struck the typewriter like a foundry bell, and every key released a worker, a drummer, a prisoner tunneling through the grammar of the republic. from newark’s burning avenues to the black arts theaters where history rehearsed its jailbreak, you made language refuse the plantation manners of the page. your vowels carried harlem rent strikes, bandung thunder, malcolm’s severed daylight, lumumba’s blood flickering beneath the atlantic; your consonants marched beside coltrane into the furnace, wearing masks carved from douglass, du bois, garvey, robeson, and the unnamed millions whose bones hold up the banks.

you were not safe, and safety was never the assignment. you argued with america until its white columns sweated gunpowder. you made the poem a siren, a courtroom, a saxophone with a brick in its throat. around you, young poets learned that metaphor could kick down a door, that rhythm could remember what textbooks buried, that the mouth was both weapon and wounded country. you mentored by provocation, by example, by demanding the word become answerable to the street, the factory, the cell, the classroom, the ancestors crowding the air like red constellations.

now the republic keeps polishing its old teeth: police lights graze the windows, empire eats with ten thousand silver forks, and the poor are invoiced for their own disappearance. still, your sentences stalk the marble corridors. they turn budgets into coffins, flags into x-rays, speeches into rats fleeing a flooded basement. fearless language maker, cultural warrior, difficult elder—your voice remains a black sun over newark, burning holes through obedience. generations gather in that fierce weather, lifting their notebooks like shields, learning again that a poem must not merely describe the fire. it must ask who profits from the smoke, who struck the match, and what new world can be forged from the blaze.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Create an experimental memorial poem addressed directly to an elder Black poet who confronted racism, imperialism, and American hypocrisy throughout the twentieth century.
counterfactuals.output:
### **DEAD LETTER, WITH DRUM & REDACTION**  
*for Langston Hughes*

Langston—  
the century still has your address.

I mail this to Harlem,  
to the river,  
to every railcar where democracy  
rode first class  
while you were told  
to carry its bags.

**AMERICA, exhibit A:**  
a flag laundering blood  
in public.

**AMERICA, exhibit B:**  
a mouth saying *freedom*  
with colonies between its teeth.

You heard the gears beneath the anthem.  
You named the hunger  
before the banquet admitted  
there was a kitchen.

O elder, O witness—  
you crossed borders and found  
the same white hand  
moving the same dark pieces:

Congo / Cuba / Scottsboro / Spain—  
the map kept changing uniforms,  
never its appetite.

> [Here the archive removes a scream.]  
> [Here the archive calls the scream “order.”]  
> [Here you return the scream its name.]

Langston,  
what shall we do with a nation  
that keeps asking the dead  
to be patient?

The river answers in rust.  
The moon hangs like a question mark  
over a boarded school.  
Somewhere, a child recites a pledge  
and feels the trapdoor  
under every noun.

Yet you—  
you put laughter beside grief  
and neither surrendered.

You made a blues from the broken cup,  
a trumpet from the factory whistle,  
a passport from the page.

So this is not goodbye.

This is a knock—  
        knock—  
               knock—

on the locked door of the future.

Get up, Langston.  
Not from death—  
from our throats.

Speak through the marcher,  
the migrant, the mother counting coins;  
through every country bombed  
for its own salvation;  
through every Black child warned  
that truth is impolite.

We are still at the table.  
We have brought our names.  
We have brought the receipts.  
We have brought the unburied century.

And your chair, elder,  
is not empty:

it is occupied  
by thunder.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a spoken-word tribute that contrasts a radical poet’s kindness, health consciousness, African identity, and devotion to language with corrupt leaders, dishonest executive orders, environmental destruction, and “alternative truths.”
counterfactuals.output:
**THE POET KEPT THE TRUE NAME**

He was radical—  
not because he carried thunder in his mouth,  
but because he carried kindness there  
and refused to spit it out.

In a season of clenched fists,  
he opened his hand.  
In a country where power grew fat  
on the hunger of ordinary people,  
he watched what entered his body—  
clean water, green leaves, honest breath—  
as if health itself were resistance,  
as if every heartbeat declared:

*You will not poison me into silence.*

He was African  
not as ornament,  
not as costume for a ceremony,  
but as memory in the marrow—  
continent in cadence,  
ancestry in every vowel,  
the old drums walking upright  
inside a modern sentence.

He knew language was not decoration.  
Language was land.  
Language was medicine.  
Language was the witness  
they could not bribe.

While leaders polished corruption  
until it looked official,  
while pens signed dishonest orders  
behind guarded doors,  
while forests became figures on a balance sheet  
and rivers learned the taste of oil,  
the poet kept naming things correctly.

A lie was a lie—  
even when stamped, sealed,  
and carried to a podium.

A theft was a theft—  
even when wrapped in a flag.

A poisoned sky was not “progress.”  
A silenced village was not “peace.”  
And “alternative truth”  
was only falsehood  
wearing an expensive suit.

He would not surrender the dictionary  
to those who renamed cruelty “policy,”  
greed “growth,”  
and obedience “patriotism.”

No.

He washed the words.  
Held them to the light.  
Returned them to the people.

Justice.  
Dignity.  
Africa.  
Earth.  
Love.

He spoke each one  
like planting a seed  
in ground the powerful had declared barren.

And still—  
for all his fire—  
he was kind.

That was the revolution.

To remain tender  
when the age rewarded brutality.  
To care for the body  
when the machine preferred exhaustion.  
To honor the ancestors  
when empire demanded amnesia.  
To serve language  
when propaganda offered promotion.

So let corrupt rulers keep their decrees.  
Let them manufacture applause,  
erase evidence,  
and command the smoke  
not to rise from the burning forest.

The smoke will rise.

The river will testify.

The children will ask  
who sold tomorrow  
for one more term today.

And somewhere,  
in the disciplined music of a poem,  
his voice will answer—  
clear as clean water,  
rooted as baobab,  
gentle as a hand on a fevered brow:

*Tell the truth.*

Tell it until the order is overturned.  
Tell it until the forest stands again.  
Tell it until no counterfeit fact  
can purchase our surrender.

Tell it with an African tongue,  
a healthy heart,  
a radical kindness.

Tell it—

because language remembers  
what power wants forgotten.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Imagine the eulogy of a Black Arts Movement poet in the early Trump era. Mention Harriet Tubman, Frederick Douglass, Ida B. Wells-Barnett, W. E. B. Du Bois, Pennsylvania Avenue, Standing Rock, and end with a warning that America has no friends if it treats the poet as an enemy.
counterfactuals.output:
We gather in a season of hard winds, when old lies have been polished and placed again behind the seal of power. Yet we do not gather merely to mourn a poet. We gather to salute a witness—one who made language stand upright when the nation preferred it kneeling.

The poet belonged to the long, unbroken argument for Black freedom: Harriet Tubman moving by starlight; Frederick Douglass thundering against the conscience of the republic; Ida B. Wells-Barnett naming terror when respectable men called it order; W. E. B. Du Bois measuring the color line and refusing its verdict. The poet inherited their courage and gave it rhythm, breath, laughter, fury.

From the stages of the Black Arts Movement came words that were not decorations but instruments—drums, alarms, blueprints, open hands. Those words exposed the distance between Pennsylvania Avenue and the streets where democracy was still waiting to be born. They traveled west to Standing Rock, where water protectors reminded the world that land remembers every broken promise.

Now, in this early hour of Trump, when cruelty boasts and ignorance wears authority like a borrowed crown, the poet’s voice is not gone. It survives wherever people refuse erasure, wherever art becomes assembly, wherever truth enters the room without asking permission.

Let the country understand what stands before it. This poet was never America’s enemy, but its uncompromising mirror, its midnight bell, its demand to become worthy of its own declarations. And America has no friends if it treats the poet as an enemy.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
